utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 15th of July, 2008. Good afternoon to the accused, to the Defence counsel, to the witness, the Prosecutor and his associates, and all the people helping us out. We are to continue with the cross-examination today. Ms. Alaburic, you still have 47 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon to you. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Buntic, and everyone else in the courtroom. First of all, I would like to thank Their Honours for accepting my suggestion that the witness have a look at the documents we will be discussing today. I believe that it will help make the proceedings more expeditious.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Buntic, we stopped yesterday when we were discussing document 1D 1609. We left off discussing document 1D 1609, minutes from the meeting of the civilian HVO held on the 26th of May, 1993. We can see that you attended the meeting. The first item on the agenda was the analysis of the military -- or rather, the second item on the agenda was the military and security situation, and we can see that General Milivoj Petkovic was the one who briefed those present on the military and security situation. Do you recall the meeting and can you confirm the extent of the minutes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall the meeting held on the 26th of May. These are the minutes from the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us look at the end of the penultimate paragraph of this section of the minutes under AD1, where it says that the head of the defence department said: "In the past work of the HZ HB there has not been enough effort in all the areas such as the assistance for civilian, supply of humanitarian aid, and so on and so forth, all of these were given within the jurisdiction of the defence department." Mr. Buntic, can you confirm for us that these were affairs of a civilian nature which were by circumstances, as the circumstances dictated and contrary to the regulations, given to the purview of the defence department?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the care for the refugees, transportation, material and technical equipment for the needs of a large number of displaced persons who had by that time already started arriving in the area, I believe that the defence department was in fact very much burdened by these tasks which were of a civilian character. The Office For the Displaced Persons and Refugees had not yet started attending its duties in terms of care for refugees and displaced persons and I'm well aware of the fact that these tasks fell within the purview of the defence department.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. The conclusions that follow in the text say that: "Measures need to be taken in order to ensure continued payment of salaries for soldiers." Tell us, Mr. Buntic, do you have any knowledge about irregular payment of salaries to soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the past days I talked about the fact that throughout 1992 and in part in 1993 the municipalities or the municipal HVOs were the ones through which the HVO soldiers were paid their salaries. I believe it was only maybe in February 1993 that the HVOs, municipal HVOs, got their accounts to dispense their business. I believe that it was only in early 1993. Therefore, all the finances in 1992 and the first three months of 1993 went exclusively through municipalities and from municipalities. Only at that point was the budget of the HZ HB in the making.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in the course of 1992 and 1993, were there situations where soldiers hailing from the so-called more affluent municipalities of western Herzegovina received their salaries quite regularly and in quite high amounts, while at the same time soldiers of the HVO, for instance, in Central Bosnia, had been without pay for months?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We even held meetings on the issue and some regulations were passed for that particular issue. I know that not the affluent municipalities, such as Tomislavgrad, but others which had a great many of its inhabitants temporarily working abroad, for instance, in Germany, they paid funds to the accounts of the municipalities as aid. We know that some municipalities were unable to fund those soldiers, and in particular the municipalities in Central Bosnia were unable to pay their salaries unlike the municipalities of Tomislav and Livno which received a great deal of their funds from the sources I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, do you have any knowledge about such a situation having some sort of bearing on the mood prevailing among the soldiers and their morale?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it had a bearing. If you have members of the same army, some of whom received their salaries regularly and others receiving none, then of course you will have these soldiers communicating and interacting and becoming aware of soldiers, some of whom were receiving salaries, others who were not; and of course those who were not became discontented with the situation. There were situations where the commanders had to deal with such situation as the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, let us look at document 1D 1667 now -- 1D 1167, minutes from the HVO meeting, 28th of May, 1993. We can still see that Mr. Prlic is still absent because of the obligations that required him to be present in the transitional government. We look at item 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Madam Alaburic please repeat the title of that particular item 3 and can the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can confirm. I was present at this meeting and I believe that this was one of the two or three meetings when Mr. Prlic -- which Prlic did not attend because he was first appointed the prime minister elect who was supposed to form the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the very end of the minutes it says that at the end of the meeting support was expressed for the total of the defence effort of the HVO staff. Can you confirm that this was the case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me add something briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, please, since I'm working under time restraints, can I ask you to leave any explanations for later, if necessary. Let's look at P 2575 now. The document is already an exhibit. Minutes from the meeting -- joint meeting of the civilian HVO of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO of Mostar municipality held on the 31st of May, 1993. Those present are not listed here and that's why I'm asking you whether you attended the meeting or not.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I did. As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Then we'll skip that document. Let's go to the next document, 1D 1610, minutes from the meeting of the civilian HVO, the 10th of June, 1993. We see here that Mr. Jadranko Prlic again attended the meetings of the civilian HVO and that you were there as well. I'm interested in the second item of the agenda: The current military and security situation in Central Bosnia. We see that the head of the defence department briefed the present members of the civilian HVO on the situation and suggested at the end that the Presidency of the HZ HB be -- call a meeting and that a military council be set up comprising seven to ten members. How did that come to pass? Were there discussions at the meeting of the civilian HVO before such a proposal was formulated? Was the situation alarming or did the events on the ground call for such an urgent measure to be adopted?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between February and June 1993 - and this is reflected probably in the minutes relating to that period - one can see the difficulties that the HVO of the HZ HB was faced with. I'm also referring to the tasks within my purview. In other words, the conflicts between the Bosniaks and Croats intensified, reached their peak in Central Bosnia; later on they spread on to Mostar and Herzegovina. In a nutshell, the Muslim forces, through the BH army and the security services in Mostar and Herzegovina and Central Bosnia, tried to impose and implement their decree -- or rather, their objective of how the state structure should be organized. They wanted to establish their own districts through a military way. In that context Mr. Prlic was absent from the meetings in order to try set up a government that was based on the agreement which dictated the setting up of provinces. In other words, there was great fighting resulting in large numbers of refugees and displaced persons from these areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the extent of what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, these proposals for the introduction of urgent measures put forth by the head of the department, were they accepted, do you have any -- were they implemented, do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not implemented. The Presidency did not meet after this meeting and could therefore not have appointed such a council.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the following document, 1D 1669, minutes from the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic. It would be interesting to know if you can say so why these proposals were left unrealized.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It follows from the proposal put forth by the head of the defence department that the Presidency should meet and a council be set up due to the emergency situation prevailing in the areas I referred to, and this is something that can be gleaned from all these documents, i.e., the intensification of the conflicts. However, the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna did not meet and did not pass such a decision. Why not? Well, I find it hard to explain. None of us were authorised or had the power to call a meeting of the Presidency. We could only launch initiatives, which we did. But you will see from the minutes that Mr. Zuljevic and I on several occasions during the meetings of the HVO, as in this particular instance, it was Stojic who asked that the Presidency should meet and take certain decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, could you tell us, who was the president of the Presidency that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna throughout the period that it existed was Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Could we now please look at the next document, that's 1D 1669, the minutes from the meeting of the civilian HVO dated the 5th of July. We can see from the list of the attendees that you were present. Let's look at item 8 of the agenda, report on the military and security situation in the HZ HB, and I would like to draw your attention to the fact that this civilian HVO concluded regarding this item that at the next session the military and security situation in the HZ HB should be discussed at the next session and that the chief of the Main Staff should be invited. My question to you, Mr. Buntic, is: Do you remember this session and could you please confirm whether the minutes are accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember and I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell us whether you know if the chief of the Main Staff was indeed invited to the next session of the civilian HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe that this was the case, but I can't really remember so I can't really make any claims to that effect. But I believe that at one or two sessions of the HVO he was present, one or two. I don't know whether it was the next one or any other session, but as far as I can remember he did attend one or at most two of such sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we please look at the next document, that's 1D 1672, the minutes from the meeting of the civilian HVO. The date is the 22nd of July, 1993. We don't have a list of attendees, and that's why I want to ask you whether you, Mr. Buntic, to the best of your knowledge did attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 22nd of July, 1993. I can't really be certain, Madam, so we have to put some caveats in place here. I can't be certain that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. And it follows from these meetings that the chief of the Main Staff, General Milivoj Petkovic, my client, briefed the civilian HVO about the military and security situation; and in accordance with the minutes, that would be the second time that he attended those meetings of the HVO. Does this refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said even before that I know that he attended one or two such sessions or meetings. I believe that one of those meetings was this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we please now look at the next document, that's 4D 00471. That's the conclusion from the meeting of the House of Representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna held on the 30th of September, 1993. What I would like you to help us understand, Mr. Buntic, is item 4 in these conclusions and I quote: "The supreme commander of the army of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna -- the supreme commander of the army of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the defence ministry of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and the Main Staff are hereby ordered to take all the measures necessary to defend the Croatian people and its rights." My question to you is this: To your knowledge, did the House of Representatives have the power to issue such orders?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall having attended this meeting of the House of Representatives, but I do know that this document was passed and if we look at the powers of the House of Representatives, it was empowered to make decisions. So I think we can agree on that. But now, whether it could order or issue commands or orders to anyone, that's a completely different thing. So it could issue or make decisions, but to my mind, orders are not the kind of documents or instruments that the House of Representatives could pass. I am aware of these conclusions because I came across it in my work. I know about its existence, and as you can -- as you said yourself, what you just noted follows from it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Mr. Buntic, now regardless of the name or title of a decision, was the house of representatives empowered to make decisions that would bind the four bodies to engage in some activities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. As I said before, decisions it could make, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. Could we please look at the last document on this topic, that's P 5799, it's already an exhibit. This is the -- these are the minutes from an extraordinary meeting of the government. The date is the 9th of October, 1993. The only topic is the military and security situation in Herceg-Bosna, and we can see from these introductory parts that Generals Praljak and Petkovic and Mr. Stojic warn about the detrimental -- possible detriment of the improper application of regulations, arbitrary actions by some organs in some municipalities which affect the morale of the soldiers and the combat-readiness of the troops, and primarily because of the fact that the unified financial system is not functioning which affects the equal financial status of all the members of Herceg-Bosna army, armed forces. Mr. Buntic, does this reflect what we have been talking about, about this topic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is something that we discussed over the past days and also today. You have the specific examples, the specific municipalities that were, so to speak, more affluent, that had enough funds in the budget to finance their troops, and this again affected other troops in other municipalities which did not have those funds and this resulted in an unequal status among the troops serving in the same armed forces. And people talked and they were aware of the situation. And here obviously a way out is sought to resolve the situation and to establish some kind of order here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me now move on to the topic that has to do with the set of documents marked with 3 in my binder, so if I run out of time I would like to deal with this topic which is quite important to me and I will devote any remaining time to the other topics then. Could we please look at document P 00377. This is an exhibit. This is an order issued by my client, Milivoj Petkovic, dated the 10th of August, 1992, prohibiting the entry of armed formations into the areas of responsibility and we can see that this order was issued to the military unit in Citluk too. Could you please tell us, you were the deputy commander of the military unit in Citluk, is that so, while you were in the military HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August 1992 I was no longer the deputy commander, so this is August 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 15th of May I was already appointed the head of the justice and general administration department, so before this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But on the basis of what you've told us so far and in your -- based on what you said in your testimony in the Kordic case, you did not take over as the head of the defence department but you remained active in the military HVO up until approximately the summer of 1992, and you participated in the actions launched to liberate Mostar and Dubravska Visoravan and Stolac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was about the 20th or the 21st of June, 1992, that was when I took over formally as the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is to your knowledge in the summer of 1992, in the municipalities that are listed here with the exception of Mostar, was there a military unit of the BH army present there or of any other Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say with some certainty -- with certainty that with the exception of Mostar or perhaps also Capljina, there were none. I'm not sure about Capljina so I can't be certain and rule out the possibility that there might have been some unit that was manned by Bosniaks exclusively, that I can't rule out but I can rule out this possibility for all the other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us about Mostar over the past two days, that in the summer of 1992 in Mostar there was an independent battalion operating there, it was a Muslim unit, Muslim army, but they operated under the command of the HVO in Mostar and in fact they were part of some kind of synchronised military armed force. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I attended a number of meetings that were attended by the then-commander of the defence of Mostar, Jasmin Jaganjac, he's a Muslim, a Bosniak, and I was aware of the situation. I knew that in Mostar the HVO and independent battalion were operating jointly, and the 4th Corps of the BH army grew out of this independent battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since this document was shown quite recently in the courtroom as a document purporting to show that this was meant to prohibit the Bosniak forces from entering those municipalities, so I would like us to look at 1D 1659, it was shown to you in your examination-in-chief, it was on Tuesday. Now I would like to draw your attention to the portion of the text --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just ask a little question with regard to this order. Can we take it then that the chief of the army had the power to give orders to the municipalities? That's what you have here, an order by the commander to the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is August 1992. At that time we already had the Main Staff in place and also staffs established in operational zones. So at that time, yes, the Main Staff did exist, and I don't think that this order pertains to the municipal armies or anything, it pertains to the HVO. This is an order issued to HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, Judge Trechsel, I can ask a follow-up question to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, could you please tell us who is this order issued to, who is it sent to? Who are the addressees?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the addressees are listed on the right-hand side of this document. You can see here, it says, To all the commands, to all the commanders of the military police, and to all the commanders of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And from what we can see here where it says in the lower part to be delivered to, what can we conclude based on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the municipalities that this document should be delivered to. So to all of those bodies in all of those municipalities, that's the way I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. And if you allow me then to make a conclusion, that means that this order was not sent to the municipalities, meaning the municipal authorities, but it is sent to the military units and police forces in those municipalities; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I see it and I think that it follows from this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If His Honour Judge Trechsel is happy, can we move on to the next document, that's 1D 1659, could we please look at page 9 of the minutes, that would be page 7 in the English version. You can see here that the head of the defence department made the following warning after the signing of the Tudjman-Izetbegovic Agreement a meeting was held in Sarajevo attended by Mr. Blaz Kraljevic, the then-commander of the HOS, and it was agreed that the HOS should urgently take over the power from HVO in the territories of Capljina, Ljubuski, and other municipalities. The date for these minutes is the 14th of August, 1992. Could you please tell us, Mr. Buntic, do you have any knowledge about this information, that the HOS was supposed to take over power in the municipalities of Ljubuski, Capljina, and others. These are some of the municipalities listed in this order issued by my client, General Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do know about this. I know about the tensions that resulted in the municipalities of Ljubuski and Capljina, where in particular in Ljubuski there was a threat of large-scale conflicts and great casualties, because at that time there was an HOS unit in Ljubuski, maybe 300 to 500 strong, and the conflicts threatened to break out in those municipalities, in particular in Ljubuski. I know that a great deal of effort was put in to calm those tensions down, to a lesser extent in Capljina, but the worst conflicts threatened to break out in Ljubuski so I know about that for this reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us go back to the topic that is marked with 2 in your binder. These are criminal proceedings before courts. You are an expert although you say that you're not an expert in criminal law, but I'm sure that you will be able to give me answers to the questions that I will ask you. First of all, a theoretical question, so to speak. In criminal procedure law in the former Yugoslavia, was there a distinction between the principle of legality and the principle of opportunity in criminal prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The principle of legality meant the application of legal norms as they are formulated, whereas the principle of opportunity, the way I see it, is the principle whereby norms that represent all the qualities or characteristics of criminal offence, if such a criminal offence does not pose great danger to the society, then it is not treated as a criminal offence, as a felony, but as a misdemeanour because we had situations --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you since I remember quite well the definitions from our textbooks and we are the same generation, that's not how it is. The principle of legality would imply in criminal procedural law of the former Yugoslavia that the public prosecutor is duty-bound to undertake criminal prosecution whenever there is enough evidence indicating that a certain person perpetrated the criminal offence that must be prosecuted ex officio. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in criminal procedural law, yes. What I was trying to explain earlier would have to do with substantive criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, the Law on Criminal Procedure, which was a federal law applied in all of the republics of the former Yugoslavia, did it apply the principle of legality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was contained in the federal Law on Criminal Procedure of Yugoslavia which was taken over as such through a decree passed by Bosnia-Herzegovina and later on by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as we were able to see from the evidence adduced before this Tribunal earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did this mean that according to the law the public prosecutor was duty-bound to undertake criminal prosecution or certain actions, not only on the basis of a criminal report but also on the basis of any other relevant information to the effect that a certain individual had committed a certain criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember the definition from the Law on Criminal Procedure, it stated approximately the following. Where a prosecutor comes to learn in whatever way that a certain criminal offence has been committed, he is duty-bound to take certain actions prescribed by the law in order to ascertain whether a criminal offence has indeed been committed; and if so, that the perpetrators thereof be punished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Almost a literal quotation. Mr. Buntic, for Their Honours who are only now hearing about the criminal prosecution as practiced in the former Yugoslavia from the various witnesses, can you tell us what the role of the bodies of the Ministry of the Interior in the criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role was to detect criminal offences committed, the perpetrators thereof, and to file criminal reports against the perpetrators of criminal offences. Where the latter are not known, then they have to take measures to identify the perpetrators. Based on an order from the prosecutor, they were duty-bound to take certain actions to gather information as required by the prosecutor, who in turn had his duties and obligations prescribed by the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Apart from that, all the state bodies and the officials in those bodies, did they have the obligation to make sure that the crime scene be secured and that all the evidence recovered at a crime scene be properly preserved?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the office holders, even in municipalities, were duty-bound by the criminal procedure law to report an offence if it had been committed in the territory of their municipality. This was a duty also held by everyone who came by that information, even if they worked in the socially owned companies and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since this answer is in full accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure, I do not see it fit to waste my time to show Mr. Buntic the relevant provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure. However, I should like to draw Their Honours' attention to the fact that what the witness has just said is contained in Articles 148, 151, 152, 154, 162, 163, and 164 of the law. Mr. Buntic, let us see how these obligations were exercised before military courts, in the military judiciary. I will put questions to you, and if I will think that some of your answers are unclear, we will see how the decree on the district military courts resolved the matters. Tell us this: The obligation that we referred to as the obligation of all the state bodies and the officials employed in them, was it in a way translated in the -- into the decree on district military courts as the obligation of the commanders of military units to preserve all the traces, prevent the perpetrators from absconding, and take -- and take all the other measures to ensure that prosecution be carried -- conducted?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me just state that Article 27 of the decree on district military courts regulates this. This is Exhibit P 00592, an exhibit therefore. Tell us, Mr. Buntic, who discharged the role of the body of the internal affairs before the military courts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the decree, if the civilian police appeared before civilian courts, then by that analogy the military police appeared before the military courts. In most of the cases that we were able to see, the criminal reports that ended up before the military courts was filed by the military police. We were able to see that in some cases it was even the military police of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at Article 25 of the decree on district military courts, document P 592. In the penultimate paragraph it is stated that: "The tasks of the organs of the interior shall be discharged by the authorised persons of the security organs of the armed forces." Tell us, Mr. Buntic, you mentioned military police. Were there any other security organs or bodies within the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there was the security service in addition to the military police. I believe that it was called SIS for short.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we conclude on the basis of the decree that SIS was also authorised to discharge the roles of the bodies of the internal affairs before the military courts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this follows from Article 25 of the decree.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you for these answers. Let me just state that the Law on Criminal Procedure is a document that was used yesterday during the cross-examination led by Madam Senka Nozica under number 4D 01105.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now ask to be told how much time I have still have left, if any, so that I can organize my examination for the next five or six minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the registrar, but it's probably not a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I correct the transcript at page 9 [as interpreted], line 22, I would like to talk with this witness for a long time, but five or six months would be taking it a bit too far.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To stay here that long?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: To get the record right, it was page 19, not page 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 19, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've used one hour and 24 minutes, so if I'm not mistaken you have six minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I should like to discuss with you events related to a date that at least for the defence of General Petkovic is a crucial date in the case, namely, the 13th of June -- the 30th of June, 1993. Does this date stand out as of any importance in the relations between Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying right now to recall how the events unfolded from the beginning of March onwards in 1993. Some conflicts broke out even earlier on, at the end of 1992. However, the 30th of June is a date that I cannot identify in terms of what happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Buntic, did you ever hear that sometime in mid-1993 the HVO lost control over an area in eastern Mostar, to the north of Tihomir Misic barracks, including the barracks itself, as a result of an attack by the BH army and that Muslim soldiers of the HVO also took part in the attack who simply changed sides overnight?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with these events. You've just reminded me of that time. I'm -- wasn't sure whether this indeed happened on the 30th of June. I am, however, aware of that event. There was a truce signed earlier on between the Muslim and Croats sides in Mostar. As a result of that, the Tihomir Misic barracks was earmarked for the HVO soldiers for billeting the HVO soldiers, whereas the Muslims were supposed to be billeted at the Konak barracks. I'm not sure about the name of the barracks, however. I know that such an agreement was signed for the respective armies to withdraw into the two barracks, the HVO forces into the Tihomir Misic barracks and the BH army forces into the Konak barracks - again, I'm not sure about the name. Shortly afterwards, an attack was launched against the barracks where, according to the agreement signed, the HVO soldiers were supposed to be billeted. It was much talked about, this attack, in the context of a part of the HVO members of Muslim ethnicity taking part in the attack after having changed sides overnight. This was an attack from within, so to speak, and the result was the loss of the Tihomir Misic barracks located in -- on the eastern bank of the Neretva in the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Buntic, did -- had you ever heard before that point that a resident would not be allowed to become a member of the HVO because he was a Muslim or of Islamic religious affiliation and that any sort of discrimination had been implored against the Muslim members of the HVO, of the members of the HVO who had been members theretofore?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you with full responsibility that in the early days in the 1992 the HVO was the only multi-ethnic military force in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Among the ranks of the HVO in Herzegovina, some 30 per cent of members were Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my cross-examination is completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Buntic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question I would like to put to you with respect to the meeting of the Croatian Defence Council or to the meetings, and we have all the minutes of these meetings because most of the time you attended them. The Defence counsel has just pointed out the fact that during these meetings civilian matters were also dealt with, and we saw that General Petkovic took the floor during these meetings to report on the situation. But when you look closely at these minutes you realize that no military operations plan is mentioned in relation to the movements of the enemy, of the ABiH. In your view, were there meetings where strictly military matters were discussed, meetings that would have taken place somewhere else; and if you know, can you tell us who attended these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the precise number, but I believe that there were over 50 meetings of the HVO, of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; and to the best of my recollection the commander of the Main Staff, General Petkovic, attended perhaps one or two of these meetings, as far as I can remember. And this normally happened in situations where the military situation was quite complicated and the attacks of the enemy side were looming, and that's why the military representative would be invited to brief on the situation. The civilian HVO which we discussed in the course of the day in terms of the civilian -- being a civilian body of the HZ HB did not have the power to issue orders which had to do with operational activities of the army. We said that in accordance with the regulations of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and de facto, such powers were vested with the supreme commander of the armed forces of the HZ HB, Mate Boban, as the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and that these powers of his stemmed from the regulations but they also existed de facto. He was the immediate superior of the -- to the Main Staff. He could issue orders to the Main Staff, which in turn could forward these orders to the commanders of the operational staffs and so on and so forth. Let me not go into the military structure because in June 1992 I did not take part in these activities and I should not like to speak about the structure of the army after the 20th of June, 1992. But I believe this was the chain of command that existed in reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this mean that for all military issues, military operations, deployment of forces on the ground, military strategies or defence or -- defensive or offensive actions, there were other meetings held by Mr. Boban and the military without you or Mr. Prlic or the civilian HVO taking part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I can say with 100 per cent certainty is that I myself never attended any such meetings. I said that after the 20th of June, 1992, that was the case. I can speculate or assume, but I cannot tell you anything else apart from what I've already told you. But I believe things did unfold as they were regulated by the decree, and I also know that Boban would not allow anyone else to exercise command over the army because he was the supreme commander. I know, Your Honour, that there existed some units that neither Boban nor the Main Staff were able to put under their control, and I know that there were conflicts because of that, a number of incidents that threatened to escalate into large-scale conflicts that would have major consequences. I don't know whether this was the thrust of your question, but I'm aware of those incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're not quite answering my question. Let me take an example. On the 10th of June, 1993, there was a meeting that started at 11.00. Prlic, Zubak, Stojic, you, Tadic, Maric, Didjic [phoen], Kelcic [phoen], and Soljic attended. I named all the participants. Mr. Stojic reported on the military situation to all the participants, this situation being serious. Very well, you can imagine Mr. Stojic reporting on it. The participants of the meeting must have asked themselves, given the seriousness of the situation, how they could face it, militarily speaking. Did they have enough forces to resist the ABiH offensive, what were they going to do, what kind of strategy were they going to adopt, and so on and so forth. This does not appear in the minutes, so a logical Cartesian mind is bound to conclude or infer that that must have happened somewhere else, there must have been other meetings with other participants that are going to work out the strategic and military issues for defensive or offensive purposes. That's what I want to know. As far as you know, were there other meetings held by Mr. Boban with the relevant military individuals dealing with these operations, otherwise the impression one gets is that it's your -- everything was settled in your meetings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as you said yourself, a sane mind would have to draw this conclusion and my knowledge is based on my stay in the army, and at that time decisions were made in such a way. Meetings were held with the Main Staff, they were attended by Boban, and in operational sense, orders were issued at that level, at the meetings that were attended by Mr. Boban, the commander of the Main Staff, and the commanders of the zones, for the most part. So when we're talking about operational activities of the armed forces, I'm saying that on the basis of my experience, my service in the army. And after the 20th of June, I no longer attended those meetings. But I do have this experience to draw on up until that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, I would like to ask you a question which may be a bit theoretical and does not relate to what we've heard today immediately. But I remember having seen a decree on the establishment or law, a draft law, on the establishment of districts and we've been told that that was never materialised, those districts were not in fact created. On the other hand, as far as the organization of the judiciary is concerned, we have heard that there existed district courts. I would be grateful if you could explain what the district in district courts refers to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this issue was discussed, and we probably have to now go back to the very beginning, the point of origin, and that would be the meeting between the two presidents, Tudjman and Izetbegovic, in Medjugorje where some agreements were reached and I think that this document is in the possession of this Court. I assume that it has already been admitted into evidence and that I should not now discuss it at length. But one of the provisions of this agreement stipulated that obligations would be undertaken to bring in line the regulations of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna with those of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that one of the items of this agreement was to that effect. I also testified here that the decree on the establishment of courts dated the 3rd of July was suspended -- its publication was suspended, it was never actually published and it was never actually implemented in practice. After that I had talks with the justice minister of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- or rather, the deputy minister, not the minister but his deputy, that was so officially but in actual fact he was the minister, where we tried to find ways to establish a judicial system that would be able to function. So I can now say that at the beginning of our talks there was complete rejection of our proposals for the judicial system in Bosnia and Herzegovina to be set up in this manner, but as -- if you follow the developments you will see that the model that was finally applied was the one that me and Mr. Halilagic actually agreed on. So on the basis of the agreement of the two heads of state and the agreement between Buntic and Halilagic, this was done in this matter. And because the Supreme Court could not operate in its seat, the Presidency made this decision to set up and relocated departments of the Supreme Court for the area of Bihac, Tuzla, and I think there was another area. But at any rate, these two will serve by way of an example and also the relocated department of the state public prosecutor's office. So we wanted to set up a judicial system that could function in practice, because it was quite obvious that legal remedies cannot go to and from the Supreme Court in Sarajevo and the military courts. So this is as far as the Supreme Court and the public prosecutor's office is concerned. That is why district military courts were set up. As you could see, we had four such district military courts, the one in Mostar, the district court in Livno, the district court in Bosanski Brod which could not operate there which is why it was physically located in Orasje, and the district military court in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. That's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may be good to have a break before the cross-examination by the Prosecution. Ms. Alaburic, the issue of the 30th of June, 1993, was a new topic that had not been dealt with during examination-in-chief. The Trial Chamber will therefore look into the issue of the time allocated. Well, it's best to have the break now, a 20-minute break, and then -- unless you want to say something now, Mr. Stringer? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted through the Trial Chamber to ask the Defence teams one question while we're all here together that would be of assistance to the Prosecution on an unrelated matter. There's a pending interlocutory appeal that relates to the issue of potential contact between an accused and his counsel during the time that an accused may be testifying. And the Prosecution is in the process of preparing its response because two of the accused have -- I'm sorry, the Prosecution's filed its appeal. Two of the accused have filed responses. It would help us if we knew if additional accused were intending to join or file responses so that we could build into our timing the possibility of filing a single, joint reply to all of the accused. And so while everyone's here together, I wanted to ask that of all the Defence teams, whether anyone else is intending to file a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, to everyone in and around the courtroom. We have no intentions of either joining or replying in particular. I think the Court made its decision, the Prosecution is entitled to appeal, and that's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's 1D. 2D.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My reply would be the same as that of my colleague Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D -- well, first 3D.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Prosecution mentioned that two Defence teams have filed such motions to save time, that was the Defence of General Petkovic and the Defence of General Praljak, so we have already filed responses. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. We do not intend to file any response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And 6D.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will not be filing any responses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, Your Honours, just one explanation regarding the topic of the 30th of June, 1993. I would like to draw your attention to the fact that this date is related to documents that were shown to this witness in the examination-in-chief, that's the minutes from the meetings of the civilian HVO held on the 19th and the 20th of July, 1993, that pertain to taking care of persons detained in the municipality of Capljina. The detention of these people started as a result of the events of the 30th of June, so my short and simple question had to do with all the topics related to detention centres that were raised in the examination-in-chief. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will examine this very carefully. Well, you've received your answers, Mr. Stringer, there's not going to be any other filing but for the two that have already been done. We shall break for 20 minutes and we shall resume around ten to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before give the floor to Mr. Stringer, I'd like to say that the Trial Chamber discussed the issue whether the 30th of June was going to be a new topic. Well, the Trial Chamber deems it is and it adds that it's not because a subject is mentioned in a document that it allows a Defence counsel as part of the cross-examination to deal with the topic. Cross-examination only goes to topics that have been previously dealt with during the hearing, the testimony of a witness. Therefore, the time devoted to the 30th of June is going to be regarded as a new topic. Mr. Stringer, you may proceed. You have several hours at your disposal. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask how much time I do have. I'm under the assumption that it's at least seven hours for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, based on my calculations you had seven hours and 15 minutes. You see, I sleep with my calculator. It's very complicated indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Buntic. My name is Douglas Stringer, I'm an attorney with the Prosecution, I'll be asking you questions. You should have -- in your area there are four binders that constitute, hopefully, the universe of documents that I'll be referring you to during the course of your cross-examination. And before we get into the real meat of your testimony, I want to go to one more preliminary matter and I want to ask you to take the fourth binder, binder number 4. All of the exhibits marked with a D, the Defence exhibits, are in the -- I believe the last binder. Mr. Buntic, if you could turn to 1D 01184, please, 1184. 1184 --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could the usher please assist. Thank you. Binder number 4. 1D 01184.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Buntic, these were shown to you during the cross-examination that was conducted by Ms. Nozica, I believe, counsel for Mr. Stojic. Do you recognise these are the minutes of the 35th Session of the HVO held on the 9th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And your testimony yesterday was that these on page 5 at least of the English version, the minutes were erroneous in that there was an indication that individuals had been appointed at the proposal of the HVO department of justice and general administration. Do you recall that testimony about this being erroneous minutes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall that, and I said yesterday that we had had a proposal from Orasje --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Actually --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- with --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- and I don't mean to be rude, but my question relates less to the substance of the proposal and more to the procedure involved in the making -- in the adoption of the minutes. And so if I could just ask you, then, to set that document aside for the moment, that being 1D 01184, which are the -- as you say the erroneous minutes. And now if you could go to a different document which is in binder 3 which is P 02181.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And while we're going there, Mr. President, I can assure you that once we get into the flow of things we'll be moving fairly consistently through the binders without jumping around very much, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Buntic, you were not shown this document previously during the course of your testimony. Would you agree with me that this is an invitation or an announcement issued by the president of the HVO, Dr. Jadranko Prlic, that relates to convening or summoning the 37th Session of the HVO and scheduling that meeting for the 5th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have now looked at the document and I think that this is also a document that originated from the HVO. I can see that this meeting is announced and that an agenda was put forward. I can see that it is the 4th of May, 1993, but I can't see that this meeting was really held --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, well, if you'll allow me --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or that any --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you'll allow me I'll try to take you there. The question simply is this: Whether this appears to be -- did you receive in your capacity as head of the department of justice and administration, did you receive documents like this from Dr. Prlic in his capacity as president of the HVO that essentially informed the department heads of the date of the next HVO meeting, indicating what the agenda would be, and so forth? This was a very -- a fairly common procedure, announcements on the -- an upcoming HVO session?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Usually a couple of days before a meeting we would receive the materials for the meeting with the proposed agenda. As you could see from the minutes, it would happen often that the agenda would be supplemented, amended --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this was probably physically done by the HVO secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And so then here we have a notice dated the 4th of May informing the members of the HVO of a meeting, the 37th Session that would be held on the 5th of May. And documents like this were issued, I believe, pursuant to the rules of procedure of the HVO HZ HB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the case. I think I did explain about the way that the documents were forwarded and how this whole thing functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, item number 1 on this proposed agenda relates to the draft minutes of the 35th and 36th HVO Sessions. Do you see that? If you can just indicate yes or no and I'll ask you some more about that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would follow from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then turning to the end of the document, the last paragraph, Dr. Prlic indicates that this document is then accompanied by the report of the 35th and 36th Sessions so that you and the others would have an opportunity to review those minutes before, actually, the commencement of the 37th Session; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That was the usual practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So the previous exhibit, 1D 01184, you don't have to look at it but the minutes of the 35th Session, it appears that those were provided to you in advance of the 37th HVO Session that was held or to be held on the 5th of May, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'm raising this because this relates to a question that was put to you yesterday by Judge Mindua about the possibility or the opportunity for approval or correction of the minutes. Now, if I could just send you back to the other binder, the fourth binder there, for one final document on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's the binder that's on the table there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if you would turn to 1D 1607. Sir, if you could look this over and tell us, does this appear to be the minutes, then, of the 37th Session of the HVO held on the 5th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you were present at this session?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And item number 1 on the agenda was the minutes of the 35th and 36th Sessions; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then turning the page, at least in the English version, item number 1 indicates that there were no remarks to the presented minutes of the 35th and 36th Sessions and that they were then unanimously adopted. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that and it is indeed correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So that at least in respect of these minutes of the 35th, I know you said they were erroneous but you did have an opportunity to review them; and at the time that you could have changed them you did not change them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct and that's what I confirmed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the procedure related to the approval of minutes of previous sessions, is this the same procedure that applied in general to all the minutes, they would be distributed in advance and then voted upon for approval unless there were objections to them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, that was the usual practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could put that binder aside, Mr. Buntic, I'm going to take you now to the first binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think we'll be staying in this binder for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Before I direct you to any specific documents in there, Mr. Buntic, I want to ask you just a few questions about your background and very early time of your association with the structures and the leadership of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Now, I understand that originally you called Citluk, the municipality of Citluk, as your home, that's where you were raised; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. I was born there, that's where I grew up, and I spent most of my life in Citluk except for the time of my studies. I studied in Zagreb, and I worked for a short period of time in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And on your return then from Zagreb to Citluk you established a law office, and if I understand correctly, you're not really a criminal law practitioner and have not been in the past. Your resume or your area of expertise relates more to the criminal [sic] law. Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, neither of these statements is correct. I graduated in 1978 in Zagreb, and before I launched my law office I worked in three companies in Citluk. That was up until 1989 when I launched my own law office in Citluk. And from that time until the war I worked as an attorney-at-law. And the second claim is not correct because I think that I've already stated before this Court that I specialize in commercial and trade law and that 90 per cent of the cases that I did as a lawyer pertained to this area and that in my practice I may have dealt with only one or two criminal cases, but those were not any major or famous cases. I think you could term them insignificant. And I have also testified before this Court that I don't consider myself to be an expert in criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I thought that was my question, but I may have said it unclearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have, in fact, misspoken and you said that he was a specialist in criminal law, so that's what the record and my memory say, line 22 on page 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, it was my understanding that your specialty is commercial law or civil law and not criminal law; is that correct? Just so we've got it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you've got it right now, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, turning to the period of the beginning of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia and in your part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you -- beginning in 1991 and then further on into 1992, you were not a member of the HDZ political party, that's -- I believe that was your testimony at least in the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. In addition to that, I also said that I had never been a member either of the League of Communists of the former Yugoslavia or of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were, however, a member of a different party called the Croatian Democratic Party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. At the first democratic multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the representative of the Croatian Democratic Party for Citluk and as such I was on that ticket and was elected into the Municipal Assembly of Citluk with another member of the Croatian Democratic Party. In a word, we got two seats in the Citluk Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if I understand correctly, General Praljak who I believe you also knew at the time of the conflict in 1992, General Praljak was also a member of the Croatian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I knew General Praljak from my days as a student. We remained very good friends, we also had family ties. General Praljak is my son's godfather and I believe it only proper that I should state it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You also were acquainted from the early days of your youth, as I understand it, with Mr. Mate Boban, who then later was the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely not correct. I got to know the late Mate Boban perhaps in 1990 when we were contemplating the idea of setting up a political party in Herzegovina which would have been called the Herzegovinian Democratic Party. I was in charge of most of the activities revolving around the launching of this party, and Mr. Boban attended some of these meetings which is where we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then in May of 1992, as I understand it, it was Mr. Boban who offered you the position of head of the justice department in what was at the time being formed, that is, the structures of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That was between the 10th and the 15th of May, 1992. The meeting was also attended by the then-president of the Citluk municipality, Milan Lovric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then as I understand it, you didn't actually assume the position of head of the justice department until later, after the successful operation against the units of the JNA, end of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I said that it was either on the 20th or on the 21st of June, 1992, that was when I took up my duties in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony in this case you indicated that you had been elected to the Crisis Staff in the Citluk municipality and that the Crisis Staff corresponded to the Law on All People's Defence and the Law of Citluk municipality. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It is true that on the critical day when the tanks of the Yugoslav Army were stopped at Polog near Mostar, an emergency meeting of the Executive Council of the municipality of Citluk was called and the Crisis Staff was set up. It is true that I said that individuals were appointed to that Crisis Staff in accordance with the Law on All People's Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can repeat that by virtue of the duties that they discharged, these included the president of the municipality, the president of the Executive Council of the municipality, chief of the staff of the Territorial Defence of Citluk, the chief of police of the municipality of Citluk, the chief of the civilian protection staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and these were individuals - please let me finish my sentence - who in accordance with the Law on All People's Defence and in accordance with the statute of the Citluk municipality had to become members of the War Presidency which would be set up in times of war and in times of an imminent threat of war. It is also true -- please let me finish - that other members --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I apologise for cutting across you like this, but you're actually giving us a great deal more detail than I need and I think what the Trial Chamber requires, and if the Trial Chamber wants more information I'm sure they will ask you. My simple question is this: You were on the Crisis Staff and you considered the Crisis Staff at the time to be the legally constituted body and municipal body in Citluk based on the law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the Crisis Staff. This was the Executive Council, and that was later on confirmed by the Municipal Assembly which had appointed me to the Crisis Staff. I do believe that it was fully in accordance with the Law on All People's Defence and the statute of the Citluk municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And I read in your Kordic -- your testimony in the Kordic case that during this period, we're talking roughly about 1991 and into 1992, Muslims and Croats throughout other areas also set up Crisis Staffs in their own municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I believe that in the area of western Herzegovina all the municipalities set up their own respective Crisis Staffs between 9 and the 15th of May. I also believe that shortly afterwards other municipalities in Herzegovina also set up their own Crisis Staffs on the similar or -- principle or the principle that was identical to the one used in Citluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the rest, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could direct you to an exhibit in the binder, that is P 00070, P 70. It should be one of the tabbed documents at the beginning. And I don't know whether you've seen this document before, Mr. Buntic, or not. You indicated that you had a discussion with Mate Boban in November of 1992 about becoming the head of the justice department. Is that pretty much your first contact or involvement in any conversations related to the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or its governmental organization?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, this is the first time I see this document. I said that I was in contact with Boban in 1990. I think this is the first time I see this document. I haven't read it, I don't know the substance of it, but I see it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's go through it and I'll ask you a couple of questions about it, recognising that you have not seen it before but also recognising that you had some discussions with Mr. Boban during this period of time. This document is called: "The conclusions of a joint meeting of the Herzegovina regional community and the Travnik regional community." It was held in November of 1991, on the 12th. And there are a number of conclusions that then are spelled out in the document, and if I could direct your attention to paragraph 1 under the heading of conclusions. You'll see that one conclusion is that: "The Croatian people in this region and all of Bosnia and Herzegovina still support the unanimously accepted orientation and conclusions adopted in agreements with President Dr. Franjo Tudjman on 13 and 20 of June, 1991, in Zagreb." And then the passage continues on making reference to other meetings and conclusions throughout other -- the fall of 1991. And then culminating in a statement that says: "These two regional communities have unanimously decided that the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina must finally embrace a determined and active policy which will realize our eternal dream, a common Croatian state." And then it continues with the reference to proclamation of a Croatian Banovina in Bosnia-Herzegovina and holding of a referendum on joining the Republic of Croatia. So now my question to you, Mr. Buntic, is -- I guess my first question on this is whether based on your conversations with Mr. Boban during this period of time, whether you were aware of these conclusions and objectives of the individuals represented or referred to in this document.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I haven't seen the document before. You should also know that at the time, that is, in November 1991, Boban and I were political opponents. He belonged to one party, I belonged to another. I don't believe that Boban would exchange with me any political views or try to take up a common political position with me because at the time he was a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And at some subsequent time then, after you became associated with the HVO as the head of the justice department, did Mr. Boban or any of the other leadership of Herceg-Bosna share with you any aspirations, any objectives, related to the establishment of a Croatian Banovina for the ultimate connection or linking of these territories to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've already testified before this Tribunal as to the documents that were handed to me on the 20th or the 21st of June when I took up my position of head of the justice and general administration department, and I stand by what I said fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, sir, that if that was in fact a policy during this period of time, November 1991, if that was a policy of the Croatian democratic -- I'm sorry, the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you would not have known of that policy because you were not a member of the party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BUNTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that what you said is correct. In 1991 we were political opponents and it is not proper to ask of me to interpret the conclusions or views held by the Croatian Democratic Union in 1991. I don't think it will be proper of me to do that. We were political adversaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit in your binder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, just a technical question, Mr. Buntic. This document speaks of the "Croatian regional community." Are you conversant with this expression, with this term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. If you're referring to the heading of the document, what is mentioned here is the Herzegovina regional community and the Travnik regional community. Therefore, this is something that preceded the setting up of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. However, do not expect me to interpret documents which were drafted by other parties at the time, and it would not be correct of me to interpret their views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I absolutely accept that. I was only a bit intrigued by this term, and contrary to what you assume, I did not quote from the title but from the beginning of the conclusion number 1. That is where you read "Croatian regional community." But thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am particularly opposed to the use of this document. If you look at the original document, the upper left-hand corner reads "transcription of a copy." I don't think this is merely an issue of semantics. As a lawyer, I cannot even begin to imagine what a transcription of a copy might mean. What I can conceive of is that the original is absent. If you look at the next page you have allegedly three signatories, the court reporter and purportedly also Mate Boban, but none of them signed the document. It is quite odd that the conclusions from such a meeting would not be signed by anyone. If it is a transcription, it is customary practice in our parts to put the abbreviation VR, meaning as signed. So this doesn't fit with the customary practice that I'm familiar with. Now, if we look at the heading there are two communities there, the Herzegovina regional community and the Travnik regional community and then the Croatian Democratic Union below that. Based on my experience from this case and other cases, I have never seen a similar document. Alternatively, the Prosecutor should provide a foundation testifying to its authenticity. Let me also state, Your Honours, that as you were able to see with a great many documents, this document does not bear the stamp of the Croatian state archives, as many others did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you seem to be challenging the written decision by the -- of the Chamber by which it admitted this document on the 11th of December, 2007. Unless I'm mistaken, this document was admitted into evidence. Is that correct, Mr. Stringer? I was about to ask you where this document came from, but now I see that this document was admitted. I can't remember it because we've admitted thousands of documents, but Mr. Kovacic probably challenged the admission and the Trial Chamber issued a ruling that will be given to me by the Chamber's Legal Officer within a few seconds. Am I correct, Mr. Stringer? The Trial Chamber decided to admit this document following a written motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. The document is in evidence already, it's been admitted, as you've indicated, by a written decision of the Trial Chamber. That's number one. I can also say that I'm going to be going to another document that I think will also further lend weight to this particular document in terms of its reliability and probative value. So, I mean, if Mr. Kovacic wants to take the stand, I can cross-examine him about the document because he's testifying about it based on his experience here and elsewhere in other cases. I don't think it's very helpful, particularly in respect of a document that's already in evidence. But I can go to another exhibit, which I'm going to do, which I think is going to further support this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only want to reserve the right to make a subsequent filing if necessary. As I can see from the description of the document, the document was admitted into evidence pursuant to one of your decisions on a motion filed by the Prosecutor for the admission of evidence. I didn't have occasion to go through our responses, but I'm sure that we opposed the admission of such a document, although I cannot be positive about it. Even if the document is admitted, I can object to it again based on the elements that I mentioned, that is, I don't see that it is authentic. We can present the relevant evidence later on. It is now in evidence. We can challenge it and then it will be up to you to weigh the probative value thereof. As for what my learned friend said about me testifying, I dissociate myself from what he said. I am not testifying at all. I'm merely stating the elements which to me, an experienced lawyer, indicate that the document is not authentic.
